# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

---

## Editor's Preface

I will be brief, as the letters themselves deserve the reader's full attention and I have no wish to interpose myself between Hideo-sensei's words and those who will receive them.

In the autumn of 1961, at the Tenth All-Japan Championship of Swordsmanship held at the Nippon Budokan, Hideo Takashi — then thirty-four years of age, then holder of the title for six consecutive years, then widely regarded as the most complete kendōka of the postwar era — forfeited his final match. He was facing me.

I should note, for readers who have come to this collection through literary rather than martial channels, that the match was not ceremonial. It was the championship final. I had defeated four opponents to reach it; Hideo-sensei had defeated four others. We had never faced each other in sanctioned competition, though we had trained in adjacent schools and had, on several occasions, attended the same seminars. I knew his reputation. He knew, I must assume, whatever there was to know of mine.

We took our positions. The referee called *hajime*. Hideo-sensei held his stance — *chūdan no kamae*, middle guard, unremarkable, correct — for perhaps four seconds. Then he lowered his shinai, stepped back, bowed to me, bowed to the referee, and removed himself from the competition floor. He spoke to no one. He offered no explanation to the judges, to his school, or to the Japanese Kendo Federation, which subsequently revoked his ranking — a decision reversed on appeal some eleven years later, though by then he had long since taken vows at the monastery of Entsū-ji in Fukui Prefecture, and the matter of rank, I imagine, had ceased to concern him.

Hideo-sensei chose, for reasons he never disclosed to me, to withdraw.

I received the title. I held it for two years before a knee injury ended my competitive career. I became an instructor. I taught for three decades at the Tōhoku Budōkan. I lived, in all visible respects, a life organized around the discipline of the sword. If that life has been built upon a foundation whose integrity I have sometimes questioned — but this preface is not the place. The letters will speak to those who care to listen.

The first letter arrived in January of 1962, approximately three months after the forfeit. The thirty-seventh and final letter arrived —

I must correct myself. I was going to write "arrived on September the fourteenth of this year," but that is not precise. It was placed in my hand by a young monk who traveled from Entsū-ji for this purpose, and who waited in my doorway until I had read it, and then bowed and departed without speaking. Whether Hideo-sensei is still living I do not know. My own health, which has been in decline since the spring, does not permit me to make the journey to Fukui to inquire, and I find — though I have spent some months examining this reluctance — that I do not wish to inquire by telephone or post.

I have held these letters in private for forty years. I publish them now not because I believe I have the right — Hideo-sensei never requested their publication, nor, for that matter, did he request their concealment — but because I have come to understand that keeping them serves no one, least of all the man who wrote them. A letter unanswered and unshared is a sword locked in its scabbard: it retains its edge, but its purpose is betrayed.

I have taken the liberty of providing annotations where context may be useful to the general reader. I have tried to constrain myself to matters of historical and technical fact. Where I have failed in this, I ask the reader's patience. Forty years is a long time to sit with another man's words, and I find that the boundary between commentary and response has, in places, become difficult for me to maintain.

A note on the calligraphy: I did consider commissioning reproductions of the original brushwork, but the cost proved prohibitive, and in any case no reproduction could convey what the originals convey. I will say only that Hideo-sensei's hand, in all thirty-seven letters, displays a discipline more absolute than any stance I ever saw him take. Each stroke is controlled to the point of severity. There is no flourish, no wasted motion, no accommodation of the brush to the writer's comfort. One sees, in the characters themselves, the hours of practice behind them — the same hours he once gave to the sword, redirected but not diminished. I confess that I have studied these letters with an attention I cannot fully justify on scholarly grounds.

The collection is presented in chronological order. I have withheld nothing.

— Saitō Kenichi
Sendai, October 2001

---

## The Letters

---

### I.

*Letter 1. January 1962. Written on plain washi paper, folded twice, posted from Entsū-ji without return address. The envelope bore only the editor's name and the address of the Tōhoku Budōkan, where I had recently begun teaching.*

---

Saitō-san,

I have taken vows at Entsū-ji. The monastery sits in a valley where the snow comes early and does not leave until April. There are eighteen monks here. The abbot is elderly and does not speak often. I sweep the courtyard each morning and assist in the preparation of meals each evening. Between these duties I sit. The sitting is more difficult than I expected.

I am told it will take ten years before the difficulty becomes unremarkable.

I do not know why I am writing to you. I will perhaps understand in time. If these letters are unwelcome, you need not respond. I do not expect a response. I am not certain I would open one.

The weather has been cold.

Respectfully,
Hideo

---

*[Editor's note: I did not respond to this letter. I read it four times on the day it arrived, placed it in the drawer of my desk at the Budōkan, and did not look at it again for several weeks. I did not understand it. I am not certain I understand it now, though I have since come to believe that the opening of a correspondence is not unlike the opening of a match: the first movement appears simple and is not.]*

---

### II. – IV.

*Letters 2 through 4, spanning February to August of 1962, continue in a similar mode and are here summarized for brevity. Letter 2 (March) describes the monastery's daily schedule in detail — the hours of zazen, the manual labor, the evening recitation of sutras — with the same flat precision one might find in an architectural survey. Letter 3 (May) notes the arrival of spring, the plum blossoms in the monastery's small garden, and includes a passage on the quality of the well water, which Hideo-sensei calls "the most honest thing I have encountered in some time." Letter 4 (August) is the first to reference the sword directly, though only in passing: "I have found a stick of approximately the correct length and weight. I do not use it. It stands in the corner of my cell. I am aware of it in the way one is aware of a sleeping animal."*

*[I note for the reader's interest that the interval between letters was irregular throughout the correspondence, sometimes weeks, sometimes months, twice exceeding a full year. I do not believe the irregularity was arbitrary.]*

---

### V.

*Letter 5. February 1963.*

---

Saitō-san,

The abbot asked me today why I came to Entsū-ji. I told him I had committed an act of cowardice and wished to understand it. He said: "Was it cowardice?" I said I did not know another word for it. He said: "Then you do not yet need to understand it. You need a better word."

I have been thinking about the nature of errors. Not errors of execution — a mistimed strike, a fumbled grip — but errors of *seeing*. There is a kind of perception that, once it occurs, cannot be unfelt. The eye lands on something it was not meant to find, and from that moment the world reorganizes itself around the discovery, and what was previously whole becomes — I am not saying this well.

In the *Gorin no Sho*, Musashi writes that the observing eye must be strong and the perceiving eye must be weak. I always understood this as an instruction to prioritize tactical awareness over intuition. I now believe he may have meant something different. I believe he may have meant that there are things one is *capable* of perceiving that one must choose not to perceive, because perception is not passive. To see truly is to act upon the thing seen. And there are acts that cannot be taken back.

But this is abstract, and I did not mean to be abstract.

The snow continues. I swept the courtyard four times today. Each time, by the time I reached the far wall, the path behind me had filled again. The abbot watched from the window and, I believe, found this instructive for me. I found it cold.

Respectfully,
Hideo

---

*[Editor's note: Musashi Miyamoto's* Gorin no Sho *(The Book of Five Rings), composed circa 1645, is the foundational text of Japanese swordsmanship philosophy. The passage Hideo-sensei references appears in the "Water" chapter, section 14. The standard translation reads: "The observing eye is strong; the perceiving eye is weak. What is far is close; what is close is far." Hideo-sensei's interpretation, while unorthodox, is not without scholarly support; see Nakamura (1954), who argues that Musashi's distinction implies an ethical dimension to martial perception that most translators neglect. I myself had always read the passage as Hideo-sensei initially did — as practical advice about focus during combat. I am no longer confident in my reading.]*

---

### IX.

*Letter 9. November 1964. This letter marks the beginning of what I have come to think of as the middle period of the correspondence, in which Hideo-sensei's focus shifts from the monastic life to extended philosophical and allegorical reflection. Letters 6 through 8, omitted here, trace this transition: Letter 6 discusses the relationship between breathing and intention; Letter 7 contains a sustained meditation on the act of bowing, which Hideo-sensei calls "the body's way of saying what the mouth cannot"; Letter 8, notable for its brevity, consists of a single question — "Do you still teach the third form of Ittō-ryū with the rear foot angled inward?" — followed by no elaboration. I did not respond to this question, as I did not respond to any of the letters. I note, however, that I adjusted the rear foot alignment in my instruction the following week, and that I have never been able to determine whether this adjustment was a correction or a concession.*

---

Saitō-san,

I will tell you a story that the abbot told me, which he claims to have received from his own teacher, though I suspect he may have invented it. You will forgive the indulgence. I have few other means of being precise.

There was once a swordsman of considerable skill who served a particular lord in a particular province. His reputation was such that challengers sought him out from distant regions. He defeated them all. He was not cruel in victory; he took no pleasure in the act of cutting. He simply saw, in each opponent's approach, the line of failure — the place where the opponent's form betrayed a fracture — and he followed that line to its conclusion. This was not genius. It was a kind of clarity he had been born with and had sharpened through decades of practice, and he regarded it the way a man with unusually strong hands might regard a jar he has opened: without pride, and with only a dim awareness that others find the task difficult.

One day his lord called upon him to spar — not to the death, but as a demonstration for visiting dignitaries. The swordsman took his position. His lord took his. And the swordsman saw, immediately and irrevocably, the fracture.

It was deep. It was fundamental. It ran through his lord's guard like a crack through the spine of a clay pot — invisible to an untrained eye, invisible perhaps to every eye but his, but *there*, structural, and unfixable. Not a flaw of practice but of the body itself: the way the lord's shoulder sat in its socket, the way weight distributed across the lord's rear hip. A flaw that meant every victory his lord had ever claimed — and his lord was a celebrated swordsman, a man whose identity was built upon his martial cultivation — had been won against opponents who could not see what the swordsman now saw.
